title: Northbridge Health x Redwood — procurement/legal: retention + audit log export terms
topics: Contract retention language (30/90/365) and deletion commitments
Audit log export scope, formats, and export retention boundaries
Legal hold and retention exceptions workflow
Baseline compliance reporting pack (SOC 2/ISO-aligned) and cadence
Dedicated vs Private deployment implications for data retention and residency
questions: Can Redwood commit to deleting audit logs/inference metadata within X days after retention expiration, and how is that verified?
What data is configurable vs fixed (platform logs, infra logs, security telemetry)?
Does exporting audit logs to Northbridge/SIEM allow them to retain longer than Redwood’s configured retention?
How does a legal hold work in practice (who can request, approval, duration, audit trail)?
Can Redwood provide a customer-ready compliance packet before signature (SOC 2 report + retention attestation + control/evidence mapping)?
action_items: Redwood (Sofia Mendes): Send redlines proposal for Data Retention & Deletion clause, including 'configurable retention' language and carve-outs for SRE/vendor logs (due 2025-02-18).
Redwood (Michael Grant): Provide proposed legal hold clause + exception workflow summary suitable for MSA/DPA exhibit (due 2025-02-18).
Redwood (Naomi Feldman): Share v1 'Compliance Reporting Pack' draft sections list + what artifacts can be shared pre-signature (due 2025-02-17).
Northbridge (Evan Brooks): Confirm required retention durations by data class (audit logs vs admin activity vs request metadata) and whether 365-day default is required or optional (due 2025-02-19).
Northbridge (Priya Shah): Confirm whether SIEM export is a must-have at launch or acceptable post-launch with interim S3/HTTPS export (due 2025-02-19).
next_steps: Redwood to send clause redlines + one-page retention/audit export summary for attachment to the security review packet.
Northbridge to respond with target retention values and required evidence list for procurement file.
Schedule a 30-min follow-up focused on audit export mechanics (formats, frequency, and retention boundary metadata).
summary: Northbridge’s procurement/legal team reviewed Redwood’s proposed retention and deletion language, focusing on commitments around audit logs, admin activity logs, and inference request metadata. Redwood clarified that retention will be tenant-configurable within guardrails (min/max) for specific datasets, and that exported audit logs are bounded by the configured retention window (exports include metadata/warnings when near boundaries). The parties discussed a legal hold mechanism (exception workflow + approvals + audit trail) and agreed Redwood will provide a baseline compliance reporting pack (SOC 2/ISO-style control-to-evidence matrix + retention policy attestations + audit log coverage summary) to reduce security review friction. Redwood will send proposed clause updates and a customer-ready documentation packet outline; Northbridge will confirm required durations (30/90/365 days) by data class.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript (auto-generated)

Meeting: Northbridge Health x Redwood — procurement/legal: retention + audit log export terms
Date: Feb 13, 2025
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 min

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Markus Klein, Sofia Mendes, Michael Grant, Naomi Feldman
Northbridge Health Systems: Janet Morales (Procurement), Evan Brooks (Assoc. GC), Priya Shah (Security & Risk), Tom Reilly (IT Vendor Mgmt)

— — —

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool. Okay, I think we’re all on. Thanks everyone for making the time. This is mainly to go through the retention language and audit log export commitments, and then what we can provide as part of the compliance packet. Sofia and Michael are here from our legal team, and Naomi from Security & Compliance product.

[00:18] Janet Morales: Thanks Markus. Yeah, we’ve got our redlines open. We want to align on a couple of points before we keep iterating in email.

[00:28] Evan Brooks: Same. We’re trying to avoid surprises later with “we can’t commit to deletion” type language.

[00:35] Markus Klein: Totally fair.

[00:38] Priya Shah: And from security, we need a clean explanation we can put in our vendor file: what you keep, how long, and what we can set.

[00:48] Naomi Feldman: Yep. That’s exactly what we’re building as part of the retention controls project. Happy to walk through what’s in v1.

[01:01] Tom Reilly: Great.

[01:03] Markus Klein: Maybe we start with the clause. Sofia, do you want to tee up where we’re at?

[01:10] Sofia Mendes: Sure. So Northbridge proposed: “Vendor will retain Customer Data for no longer than 30 days unless otherwise agreed, and will delete within 7 days after termination.” And then you had a separate section specifically for audit logs requiring 365 days minimum retention. Our current standard is: default retention windows depend on the data type, and for certain datasets we’re shipping tenant-configurable retention with guardrails. We can commit to enforcing the configured retention, but we can’t promise that literally all operational logs everywhere follow that in v1.

[01:46] Evan Brooks: Right. That’s the concern. The clause reads like a marketing statement rather than a commitment.

[01:53] Michael Grant: Understood. We can tighten it. But we need to define what data classes we’re talking about.

[02:01] Priya Shah: For us, the big ones: audit logs, admin actions, and anything that could include prompts or model outputs.

[02:11] Naomi Feldman: Just to be precise: today we do not position “raw prompts and outputs stored indefinitely.” In Hosted, we log request metadata and limited operational signals. In many cases, the raw payload content is not kept as a durable dataset. But we do have audit logs and admin activity logs that are separate.

[02:30] Priya Shah: So do you store the prompt content at all?

[02:33] Markus Klein: It depends on the feature. For example, for debugging you may enable more verbose logging, but by default, our position is to minimize retention of payload content. Naomi can confirm, but the v1 scope for configurable retention is audit logs + admin activity + certain telemetry tables, not “all raw inference payload content.”

[02:52] Naomi Feldman: Correct. For v1, we’re targeting retention controls for: audit logs, admin activity, request metadata where applicable, and analytics/telemetry that’s eligible. Some infra logs are governed by SRE standards or vendor constraints.

[03:10] Evan Brooks: Okay. Then clause needs to be explicit about that distinction.

[03:14] Sofia Mendes: Agreed. We can propose an exhibit that lists the covered datasets and the default retention and range.

[03:23] Janet Morales: We like exhibits. Procurement loves exhibits.

[03:27] Markus Klein: (laughs) We can do that.

[03:31] Evan Brooks: On audit logs: we require 365 days for certain systems, mainly for investigations. Can your product do 365?

[03:40] Naomi Feldman: For audit logs specifically, yes, 365 is within the supported max in the policy guardrails we’re planning. There will be a minimum and maximum; we’re trying to avoid “never delete.” Also there’s legal hold override.

[03:57] Priya Shah: Minimum and maximum meaning what?

[04:00] Naomi Feldman: Example numbers, not final: minimum might be 30 days for audit logs (to ensure system integrity and troubleshooting), and max might be 400-ish or 730 depending on data type. But we can align to 365 for audit logs and admin activity.

[04:17] Evan Brooks: If it’s configurable, can we set it to 365 as a term in the contract and treat that as a requirement?

[04:23] Sofia Mendes: We can commit that for your tenant the retention setting will be configured to 365 days for audit logs and admin activity logs, subject to the product guardrails, and we’ll notify you if any guardrails change.

[04:38] Janet Morales: And deletion after that?

[04:41] Naomi Feldman: Enforcement means the backend jobs and TTL policies delete or compact data after it passes the retention horizon, and we expose auditability like “last enforcement run” and exceptions.

[04:55] Tom Reilly: When you say delete, is that hard delete or like… tombstone?

[05:01] Naomi Feldman: Depends on datastore. For some, it’s partition TTL, so data becomes inaccessible and is removed during compaction. For others, it’s a scheduled deletion job. But in both cases, the intent is that it’s removed from active storage and not returned via any API or export.

[05:20] Evan Brooks: That’s exactly the language we need: “no longer accessible” plus “removed from systems.”

[05:27] Michael Grant: We can phrase it as: “Redwood will implement technical controls designed to delete or render irretrievable the covered data after the retention period, except where prohibited by law or subject to legal hold.” Something like that.

[05:45] Priya Shah: “Designed to” is the squishy part.

[05:48] Sofia Mendes: We can use stronger language for the covered data types where we have enforceable controls. For the carve-outs, we’ll list them.

[06:00] Markus Klein: Also, to be transparent, our SRE logs and some vendor-managed logs can have fixed retention (like 14 or 30 days) and you can’t increase those. But those logs are not your audit logs, they’re more like infrastructure events.

[06:17] Priya Shah: But those can still include identifiers.

[06:19] Naomi Feldman: They can include operational identifiers, yes, but we’re working to keep customer content out of those streams. And we can describe that in the compliance packet.

[06:33] Janet Morales: Let’s talk termination. Our standard is delete within 7 days.

[06:39] Sofia Mendes: For most SaaS, 7 days is hard with backups and disaster recovery. We typically commit to deletion from active systems within a defined window, and from backups within a longer window.

[06:52] Evan Brooks: What is your backup window?

[06:55] Michael Grant: Standard is up to 35 days for backups, but we can confirm per environment. For Private deployments, it can be customer-managed.

[07:08] Tom Reilly: So if we went Private, we control backups entirely?

[07:11] Markus Klein: In a Private deployment, you’re running in your VPC or on-prem. You typically control storage and backup policies, with our software layer. That gives you more control over retention and residency, but more operational responsibility.

[07:26] Priya Shah: For now we’re assuming Hosted or Dedicated, but Private is on the table.

[07:33] Markus Klein: Got it.

[07:36] Janet Morales: Okay, audit logs export. We need the ability to export audit logs to our SIEM, and we need a statement that you won’t prevent us from retaining the exported logs for longer.

[07:47] Naomi Feldman: Right. Exports: we support export of audit logs in JSONL/CSV format. For SIEM, we can integrate via HTTPS push or you can pull from an export endpoint. The key nuance: Redwood will only export what exists within your configured retention window at the time of export.

[08:06] Evan Brooks: But once exported, we can keep them forever.

[08:09] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Once exported to your system, you become the controller of that copy. We can add metadata in exports that indicates the retention policy and export time.

[08:21] Priya Shah: That’s good. We also need you to commit that the export feed won’t silently omit events.

[08:28] Naomi Feldman: The export is bounded by retention and by filters you apply. But within the available window, it’s complete for the audit log dataset. There are some events that are not in audit logs by design (like internal SRE operations not tied to your tenant).

[08:46] Priya Shah: What do you include in audit logs exactly?

[08:49] Naomi Feldman: Tenant admin actions: changes to API keys, org settings, retention policy changes themselves, RBAC role changes, SSO config changes. Also control plane actions like model enablement, route changes, dedicated capacity changes—basically actions that matter for security and governance.

[09:13] Tom Reilly: And inference requests?

[09:15] Naomi Feldman: Inference requests are usually not in “audit logs,” but there’s request metadata and usage analytics. That’s a separate dataset.

[09:24] Evan Brooks: That distinction is going to confuse our auditors. They see “audit logs” as everything.

[09:30] Markus Klein: We can provide a coverage summary: what events are in audit logs, and what’s in telemetry. It’s part of the reporting pack.

[09:41] Janet Morales: Speaking of the reporting pack, what exactly are you providing? We can’t sign with a promise to deliver “some documentation later.”

[09:50] Naomi Feldman: For v1, we’re putting together a baseline compliance reporting pack you can hand to procurement/security. It includes: a retention policy attestation per tenant (what’s configured, ranges), an audit log coverage summary, and a control-to-evidence matrix aligned to SOC 2 / ISO style controls.

[10:13] Evan Brooks: Are you giving us your SOC 2 report?

[10:16] Markus Klein: We can share SOC 2 under NDA. The reporting pack is more like a customer-friendly packet. We can do both.

[10:25] Sofia Mendes: And we’ll be careful not to over-commit in contract to deliver a “SOC 2 report” unless the NDA is in place.

[10:33] Janet Morales: Our NDA is already in place, I believe.

[10:36] Markus Klein: Yes, I think so.

[10:38] Priya Shah: For evidence, we also want proof that retention enforcement actually runs.

[10:44] Naomi Feldman: We’re building auditability: “effective policy” view, last enforcement run timestamp, error state, and exceptions/legal holds list. Not everything will be directly exposed, but we can provide screenshots and logs as evidence during audits.

[11:03] Priya Shah: Screenshot evidence is okay for SOC 2 type, but we may ask for more.

[11:08] Naomi Feldman: We can also provide an attestation signed by our compliance lead and references to internal runbooks and monitoring controls, though those are generally not shared in full.

[11:23] Evan Brooks: How do legal holds work? This is a big sticking point.

[11:27] Michael Grant: Legal hold means if there’s a litigation hold or regulatory requirement, data that would otherwise be deleted is preserved. The question is who triggers it and how it’s documented.

[11:39] Janet Morales: For us, only our legal team can request it.

[11:42] Michael Grant: That’s fine. In product, we’re implementing a legal hold flag at the tenant level for specific datasets, with an approval workflow. We can include in the contract: “Upon Customer’s written request, Vendor will place the specified data on legal hold.” And we can specify that holds override retention deletion for as long as the hold is active.

[12:05] Priya Shah: Is it self-serve? Like in console, we click “legal hold”?

[12:10] Naomi Feldman: Likely not fully self-serve in v1. It’s an exception workflow: you request, we apply, and we keep an audit trail. Longer term we can make it admin-configurable with guardrails.

[12:24] Tom Reilly: That’s probably acceptable as long as it’s timely.

[12:28] Evan Brooks: “Timely” meaning within 24 hours.

[12:31] Sofia Mendes: We can commit to an SLA for processing legal hold requests during business days, like 1 business day, assuming proper authorization.

[12:43] Janet Morales: Add that.

[12:45] Markus Klein: Noted.

[12:47] Priya Shah: Another question: if we set audit retention to 365, can Redwood lower it later without telling us? Like a platform change.

[12:56] Naomi Feldman: You control the setting within the allowed range. If guardrails changed, we’d notify. But we’re not planning to reduce maximums.

[13:07] Evan Brooks: We’d like a clause: “Vendor will not materially reduce retention functionality without notice.”

[13:13] Sofia Mendes: We can include in the change management / product changes clause: advance notice for material adverse changes. We already have something similar.

[13:23] Markus Klein: Great.

[13:25] Janet Morales: Let’s talk numbers. We see in the security questionnaire: 30 days, 90 days, 365 days. Can you support 90 for some logs and 365 for audit?

[13:36] Naomi Feldman: Yes, the policy model is per data type. So you could set telemetry to 90, audit logs to 365, admin activity to 365, request metadata to, say, 30 or 90 depending.

[13:52] Priya Shah: What is “request metadata” exactly?

[13:55] Naomi Feldman: Like timestamps, model identifier, token counts, latency, status codes, and customer org/project identifiers. Generally not full text content.

[14:09] Priya Shah: Okay.

[14:12] Evan Brooks: We need the contract definition of “Customer Data” to include or exclude those things carefully. Otherwise it’s messy.

[14:20] Michael Grant: Agreed. We can add a definition of “Service Data” or “Operational Data” that includes aggregated metrics and logs, and then specify retention separately for “Customer Content” vs “Audit Logs” vs “Operational Logs.”

[14:37] Janet Morales: We’ve seen that in other vendor agreements. Works.

[14:41] Markus Klein: Naomi, can you cover export commitments? Priya asked about completeness.

[14:46] Naomi Feldman: Sure. Audit log exports: we can commit that for the audit log dataset, exports will include all events recorded for your tenant within the available retention window, subject to filtering. We’ll also include fields like event_id, occurred_at, actor, action, target, and request_id where applicable.

[15:06] Priya Shah: Do you support signed webhooks?

[15:09] Naomi Feldman: We support signed requests for outbound delivery; otherwise, you can do pull-based export with API keys and IP allowlisting. For Private, you can push directly into your SIEM in-network.

[15:25] Tom Reilly: And formats. You said JSONL and CSV.

[15:28] Naomi Feldman: Yeah. JSONL is preferred for SIEM ingestion.

[15:33] Evan Brooks: Redwood’s clause currently says “may provide exports.” We need “will provide.”

[15:39] Sofia Mendes: For your contract, we can make audit log export a committed feature, subject to the plan/tier you purchase.

[15:48] Janet Morales: Great.

[15:50] Markus Klein: If helpful, we can attach an audit log export spec as an exhibit too.

[15:55] Priya Shah: Yes. Even a one-pager is fine.

[16:00] Markus Klein: Okay.

[16:03] Janet Morales: Another legal question: data residency. If we’re in US, can any of this be processed elsewhere?

[16:10] Markus Klein: For Hosted, you choose region and we keep data in-region per our residency controls. For Dedicated, you can pick region as well. For Private, it’s your environment.

[16:22] Evan Brooks: But do you have support personnel accessing logs from outside the region?

[16:28] Naomi Feldman: Access is controlled and audited, and we can add restrictions. But yes, support could access from other locations depending on incident response. That’s a separate access control topic.

[16:42] Priya Shah: Okay, not today.

[16:45] Markus Klein: Right.

[16:46] Janet Morales: Back to retention. We had a “no longer than necessary” clause. Are you comfortable with that?

[16:52] Sofia Mendes: As a principle, yes, but we need it to be operationalized via the configured retention schedule. So we can say: “Vendor will retain covered data no longer than the retention period configured by Customer, subject to minimum retention required for security and system integrity.”

[17:10] Evan Brooks: That’s good.

[17:12] Michael Grant: And then “except for legal holds, legal obligations, and backup retention cycles.”

[17:19] Janet Morales: Fine.

[17:21] Priya Shah: Can we get reporting that shows our configured retention? Like a screen.

[17:27] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Console will show the effective policy per dataset, including inheritance (org vs environment). Also shows last enforcement run.

[17:39] Priya Shah: What do you mean inheritance?

[17:41] Naomi Feldman: If you have multiple environments, like prod and staging, you could set different retentions. Also if you have multi-region. Policy precedence decides what applies.

[17:55] Tom Reilly: That’s more advanced than we need, but okay.

[17:59] Markus Klein: We can set defaults and you can leave them.

[18:03] Janet Morales: Competitor comparison question—sorry. Azure OpenAI gave us a standard statement: “audit logs retained 90 days.” We need 365. If we go with you, we need to justify why it’s different and why it’s okay.

[18:18] Markus Klein: Totally. Many managed services have fixed retention; Redwood is building configurability and export. So you can keep 365 in your SIEM, even if the platform retains 90. In our case, we can actually retain 365 for audit logs. That’s a differentiator.

[18:36] Priya Shah: AWS Bedrock also has limitations. So okay.

[18:41] Evan Brooks: But to be clear: you’re not saying you will keep inference prompts for 365.

[18:46] Naomi Feldman: No. Audit logs are admin/control plane. Inference payload content is different. We can discuss separately if you need longer-term content storage, but that’s not our default.

[18:58] Evan Brooks: That’s fine.

[19:00] Janet Morales: Can we add a clause: “Vendor will not use Customer Content to train models.”

[19:05] Sofia Mendes: We already have that in the DPA. We can point you to it.

[19:10] Markus Klein: Yep.

[19:12] Priya Shah: I want to revisit verification. If auditors ask “prove deletion,” what do we show?

[19:20] Naomi Feldman: We can provide: (1) your configured policy, (2) an enforcement status page showing jobs running, (3) audit events when retention policy changes, and (4) in some cases, evidence that a record older than retention is not retrievable through export queries. We also have internal monitoring on backlog and errors.

[19:44] Priya Shah: Okay.

[19:45] Evan Brooks: Would you sign an attestation annually?

[19:49] Michael Grant: We can provide a standard compliance attestation letter as part of the pack. We’ll need to limit scope to what we actually control.

[20:00] Janet Morales: Good.

[20:02] Markus Klein: We’re at about 20 minutes. Anything else on redlines?

[20:08] Evan Brooks: Just the “delete within 7 days after termination” piece. Can we get a firm timeline for active systems?

[20:16] Sofia Mendes: We can propose: deletion from active production systems within 30 days after termination, and backups within 35 days thereafter, except legal hold. That’s fairly standard.

[20:31] Janet Morales: 30 is okay. But we need it in writing and not “commercially reasonable.”

[20:37] Sofia Mendes: Understood.

[20:39] Tom Reilly: Also add: export assistance during offboarding.

[20:44] Markus Klein: Yes, we can commit to providing audit log export capability during the term and a short window after termination, like 30 days, to pull the last available logs.

[20:56] Evan Brooks: As long as it doesn’t contradict retention.

[21:00] Naomi Feldman: Right. If your retention is 365 and you terminate, you’d still only be able to export what exists until deletion occurs. So we’d schedule deletion after termination per the clause.

[21:15] Priya Shah: So you might delete sooner than 365 after termination.

[21:18] Michael Grant: Correct, because termination deletion obligations override normal retention. But you can export before that.

[21:25] Evan Brooks: That needs to be explicitly stated.

[21:28] Sofia Mendes: Yes.

[21:31] Markus Klein: Naomi, can you speak to timeline for delivering the reporting pack? Janet asked about signing.

[21:39] Naomi Feldman: We can share the outline and a draft version quickly. The full “v1” pack is targeted in the next few weeks; we’re aligning it with our retention controls rollout. But for procurement, we can provide: SOC 2 report under NDA, a short retention controls overview, and a draft control-to-evidence mapping for retention and audit logging.

[22:02] Janet Morales: By next week?

[22:04] Naomi Feldman: Yes, the draft packet components by next week.

[22:08] Priya Shah: And the final polished PDF?

[22:11] Naomi Feldman: Likely within the month. But we can give you interim artifacts.

[22:18] Evan Brooks: Okay.

[22:20] Markus Klein: There’s also a question about what’s configurable in Dedicated vs Private.

[22:25] Naomi Feldman: Dedicated and Hosted share the same control plane. Retention settings would be per tenant. Private, depending on the package, you may have more direct control over the storage and can enforce via your own TTLs; we still provide the policy model.

[22:42] Tom Reilly: Alright.

[22:45] Janet Morales: I think we’re good. Can we recap deliverables? We’re going to need actual redlines, not just talk.

[22:52] Markus Klein: Yep. Here’s what we’ll do.

[22:55] Markus Klein: Sofia will send an updated retention/deletion clause with an exhibit describing covered datasets and the configurable retention ranges and defaults. Michael will propose legal hold language including who can request and SLA for processing holds. Naomi will send the compliance reporting pack outline and what we can share pre-signature.

[23:16] Janet Morales: Perfect.

[23:18] Evan Brooks: And audit log export commitment.

[23:21] Sofia Mendes: We’ll update that section to “will provide,” and specify formats and that exports are bounded by configured retention.

[23:29] Priya Shah: Please include the “coverage summary” wording.

[23:32] Naomi Feldman: Will do.

[23:34] Markus Klein: Great. Any last questions?

[23:37] Tom Reilly: None.

[23:39] Janet Morales: Good.

[23:41] Markus Klein: Okay, we’ll follow up by early next week. Thanks all.

[23:47] (call continues with minor scheduling and goodbyes; audio overlap)

[24:05] Janet Morales: Bye.

[24:06] Markus Klein: Thanks.

[24:07] Recording ended.

Note: Fireflies sometimes truncates speaker tags after the main discussion; minor scheduling chatter omitted for brevity in this export.
